name: Competitive analysis and positioning
oneliner: Incumbent mapping, competitive posture, battlecards, and win themes built before the fight starts.
metaTitle: Competitive analysis and positioning | Techno War Room
metaDescription: We map incumbents and rivals for must-win pursuits and turn it into working material: battlecards, win themes, and the questions that reframe an evaluation.

scenarios.title: Someone already lives there
scenarios.text: The buyer has a vendor. The RFP reads like that vendor wrote it, and it is possible they did.

scenarios.title: Three finalists, one story
scenarios.text: Every finalist claims the same strengths in the same words. Nobody is positioned. Everybody is merely described.

scenarios.title: Losing without a debrief
scenarios.text: Deals keep going to the same rival, and nobody has written down why or what to change.

what: We map who you are really up against, in one pursuit or across a segment: the incumbent's grip, each rival's pitch and gaps, and where your honest advantages sit. Then we turn the map into working material: battlecards, win themes, and the questions that make an evaluation ask what your rival cannot answer well.
Everything is built from public information and your team's field knowledge, and marked clearly where the evidence is thin.

deliverables.name: Competitive map
deliverables.desc: The field for this pursuit or segment: who holds what, and where the openings are.

deliverables.name: Battlecards
deliverables.desc: One page per rival: their pitch, their gaps, the counters, and the questions to plant.

deliverables.name: Win themes
deliverables.desc: The two or three arguments this pursuit should rest on, with the proof each needs.

deliverables.name: Trap question set
deliverables.desc: Questions your team seeds into the evaluation that read neutral and cut deep.

steps.title: Frame the fight
steps.text: One deal or one segment. We agree the rivals in scope and what a win looks like.

steps.title: Research
steps.text: Public sources plus structured interviews with your sellers, who know more than anyone has written down.
steps.need: Interview time with your field team

steps.title: Map and draft
steps.text: The competitive map, the battlecards, and the win themes, drafted and sourced.

steps.title: Pressure test
steps.text: Your sellers attack the material. What survives goes into the field.

excludes: We do not gather intelligence by misrepresentation. Public information and your own knowledge only.
We do not write disparagement. Battlecards win on substance or not at all.
We do not guess numbers where there is no source. Thin evidence gets marked as thin.
We are not a market research subscription. This is working material for pursuits, not a quarterly report.

shape.v: A refresh cadence as the field moves

domains.name: B2B SaaS
domains.note: Review sites, pricing pages, and release notes make SaaS rivals unusually legible. The work is separating signal from marketing.

domains.name: IT services
domains.note: Rivals differentiate on people and price. Battlecards centre on delivery model and reference stories.

domains.name: BFSI
domains.note: Incumbency is the moat. Displacement themes matter more than feature comparisons.

domains.name: Healthcare
domains.note: Validation cycles and switching costs protect incumbents. Positioning leans on the risk of standing still.

related.name: Proposal deck building

related.name: Case study and reference development
related.desc: Every win theme needs proof. This is where it comes from.

related.name: RFP and RFI response
related.desc: Positioning decides which requirements you emphasise and how.
